documents.abstract: This study evaluated an open-weight LLM and keyword rules for title/abstract screening of circulating microRNA (miRNA) monitoring biomarker reviews. PubMed and Europe PMC searches returned 3,204 records (1,976 after deduplication). Automated keyword rules excluded 1,222 records; 754 were screened by gpt-oss-120b (n = 628) or gpt-oss-20b (n = 126) at temperature 0. One reviewer labelled 225 records; a second independently labelled a stratified 113-record sample, and 21 disagreements were adjudicated to consensus (2 Include, 3 Maybe, 16 Exclude), serving as the reference, though blinding of the first reviewer to LLM outputs could not be verified. The primary outcome was sensitivity for Include or Maybe against a pre-set threshold of 0.95. The LLM returned Include 173, Maybe 102, and Exclude 479. Against the consensus reference, sensitivity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.77–0.95), specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83–0.95), and kappa 0.65 (95% CI 0.54–0.76). Of 100 randomly sampled LLM-excluded records, 5 (5%) were reference-Include; in all five, the LLM's stated reason involved prognostic or clinical-event outcomes rather than drug response, resistance, or toxicity. Among keyword-excluded records, 11/75 (15%) were reference-Include, rising to 11/50 (22%) for the rule 'no human circulating miRNA + treatment context'. The sensitivity point estimate fell below 0.95, but its 95% CI (0.77–0.95) includes 0.95, so this pilot cannot rule out that the threshold is met; keyword pre-filters excluded relevant records at a rate that made them unsafe without audit. In this domain, an LLM can prioritise records but cannot replace human screening. The authors propose clearer outcome criteria, single-model runs, stratified human audits of every automated exclusion, and pre-registered performance thresholds.

This chapter analyzes published work on the use of large language models (LLMs) in smart frameworks for the detection and prevention of cyberbullying across social media, gaming, and learning platforms. The data shows a clear movement from the use of traditional machine learning and earlier deep learning models to the application of LLMs that possess capabilities of understanding and processing context, which allow them to identify and categorize abuses of the online environment that are subtle and implicit, as well as those that use multiple modalities and languages. The literature shows the following recurring themes: use of prompt-engineered LLMs for cyberbullying detection with little or no training; hybrid models that integrate LLMs with classical machine learning; moderation models; and conversational agents for real-time, empathetic abuse interventions. Other themes include increased focus on bias and fairness, explainability, data scarcity, and domain adaptation for high-risk systems and safety. The chapter provides this structure by first assessing foundational literature on automated detection of cyberbullying and toxic language, then LLM-based detection architectures and LLM-enabled prevention and intervention strategies, such as counseling chatbots and bystander aid tools. The subsequent sections integrate the literature on evaluation methodologies, benchmark datasets, and the spatial and temporal adversity and abusive behavior countermeasure robustness, then address the specific ethical, legal, and policy LLM online safety ecosystem deployment issues. This extensive literature review provides a synthesis of the LLM literature on online safety tools, determines converging design strategies and unresolved issues, and articulates design principles for LLM-based tools that promote safer online communities.

Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for oncology decision support, but their performance in colorectal cancer with peritoneal metastases (CRC-PM) remains uncertain. We benchmarked 10 contemporary LLMs against an expert-consensus framework. Methods Forty-eight synthetic vignettes were derived from a 2026 CRC-PM consensus guideline, including 36 primary scenarios and 12 counterfactual scenarios forming six pairs. Each model completed every vignette three times using a frozen zero-shot structured prompt. The primary endpoint was prompt-aligned structured Full concordance; contradiction-only and full-semantic adjudication were sensitivity analyses. Two blinded attending colorectal surgeons, each with 5 years of clinical experience, independently validated the reference classifications. Results Among 1,080 primary responses, structured scoring classified 609 (56.4%) as Full, 117 (10.8%) as Partial, and 354 (32.8%) as Discordant. Model-specific structured Full concordance ranged from 49.1% to 63.0%; neither the Friedman test ( P = .104) nor clustered GEE ( P = .186) supported a robust model effect. Contradiction-only scoring was similar (56.2% Full), whereas full-semantic adjudication reduced Full concordance to 45.5%. Excluding prompt-development scenarios lowered absolute concordance but did not change the inferential conclusion. Expert agreement was 93.8%–97.9% across decision domains (Cohen kappa 0.898–0.948). Counterfactual and metachronous risk-management analyses showed wide uncertainty, and 21 clinically consequential discordance flags arose from five scenarios. Conclusions LLM performance in CRC-PM was sensitive to scoring definition and did not establish a stable between-model hierarchy. Prospective clinician-plus-LLM studies are required before clinical benefit can be inferred.

documents.abstract: Product design is a complex, knowledge-based process that balances customer needs with engineering constraints and market realities. While traditional methods such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and machine learning (ML) have improved the design process and solutions, they still struggle with flexibility and a deep semantic understanding of design requirements. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), create new opportunities for intelligent, human-centred support for product design. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review analyzes 1,263 studies published between 2023 and 2026 to answer three questions: (1) how LLMs are applied across design stages, (2) how these systems are evaluated, and (3) what gaps remain. We found that LLMs successfully support design requirements analysis, ideation, and documentation. However, current evaluation methods lack standardized benchmarks for design quality. Persistent challenges remain, including hallucinations, weak domain grounding, tool-integration hurdles, and ethical concerns. To guide future research, we introduce a technical maturity map that highlights current achievements and uninvestigated areas in design systems and suggests a roadmap for applying LLMs in product design.

Through architecture, aesthetics, and material agency, ecological consciousness unfolds as a journey across scales. Thus, this book’s conclusion proposes a final time–space transscalar journey from the Paleolithic cave in France to current lunar and deep-sea explorations aimed at expanding the human condition through artificial intelligence. The ultimate demonstration underscores the urgent need to cherish and reclaim the chirotopian spaces threatened by excessive material abstraction. Therefore, the ordinary spaces within reach, fostered within architectural spaces, can not only propel the construction of a new cosmology that recognizes vibrant matter but also amplify the distinct sensibility that makes us human.

Clinical practice guidelines encode evidence-based recommendations as conditional decision flows, which makes them a natural source of process supervision for training reasoning models. Two properties of clinical reasoning make this supervision difficult to use. A decision flow consistent with a guideline does not by itself determine the correct answer for a given patient, which we call the path--answer gap, and several valid decision flows can support the same clinical decision, which we call path multiplicity. Current training approaches address parts of this problem. Answer rewards supervise the final decision, and process rewards computed against a reference flow supervise one valid decision flow per case. Supervised fine-tuning on annotated flows teaches guideline-consistent reasoning but constrains the model to one trajectory per case and can reduce answer accuracy. We introduce GUIDER, a method that jointly optimizes a decision flow controller and a reasoning policy. The controller learns to generate plausible decision flows from guideline-derived supervision, and the policy learns to generate a decision flow and a final answer for each patient case. GUIDER computes the process reward for the policy over several controller-generated flows, which accounts for path multiplicity, and gates this reward on answer correctness, which addresses the path--answer gap. Joint training allows the process supervision to evolve with the policy. On MedGUIDE, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, 3.3 and 3.1 points above the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline. With Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones, GUIDER also improves over CRPO, MRPO, and FaithMed on the out-of-domain benchmarks AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE.

documents.abstract: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds. These results show that an LLM-extraction frontend built exclusively from public knowledge can provide a representation over which evolutionary feature selection cuts the candidate feature set roughly in half without a statistically detectable cost in performance, albeit at a small point-estimate cost; that hypervolume and inverted generational distance are not reliable stand-ins for classification-relevant algorithm selection here; and that a no-gold-standard proxy evaluation can substitute human annotation when expert time is limited. Because both stages plug in and out freely, the framework can absorb stronger components in either stage as they become available.

Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable representations across different graphs and domains. However, existing GFMs face notable limitations, including limited pre-training scale or reliance on aligning with textual information in Large Language Models (LLMs). To overcome these limitations, recent studies have drawn inspiration from prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), which learn from large synthetic datasets and support multi-domain prediction backed by causal learning. However, existing graph PFNs encounter severe difficulties in modeling causal relationships within and across node and edge sets, generating diverse graph structures, and designing suitable architectures that can learn from complex synthetic datasets. To address these challenges, we propose **GSCM-PFN** (Graph SCM-based Prior-Data Fitted Network), a graph PFN pre-trained on synthetic data generated from an SCM-based prior that jointly models nodes and graph topology. Specifically, we (1) design a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model (SCM) to guide synthetic graph generation and capture causal relationships within and across node and edge sets; (2) introduce prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling to instantiate diverse graph generation strategies, and prove that our SCM-based generation prior is more expressive than existing priors; and (3) propose a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network with theoretical guarantees for learning from diverse synthetic graphs. Experiments on 23 real-world benchmarks show that GSCM-PFN outperforms both conventional GFMs and PFN-based GFMs, without utilizing real-world graph data for pre-training. Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

AI co-scientists have expanded the use of large language models for generating scientific hypotheses and guiding experimental investigation. Here we investigate whether temporal patterns in the semantic representations of complete biomedical conclusions can guide hypothesis generation. We introduce ForeSCITE, a framework that identifies thematic clusters of published conclusions, estimates a direction separating earlier from more recent findings within each cluster, and projects existing conclusion embeddings along these directions. An embedding language model trained to reconstruct conclusions decodes the projected coordinates into natural-language hypotheses. Across 407 clusters derived from approximately three million pre-cutoff conclusions, we identify temporal structure and illustrate its retention after decoding. In retrospective, time-sliced evaluations, ForeSCITE increases semantic coverage beyond the historical corpus, biomedical entity-pair novelty and post-cutoff pair re-observation relative to five prompt-based and retrieval-augmented baselines. Expert review of prioritized CAR-T hypotheses identified 37 candidates as both novel and biologically plausible, and expert justifications for five selected hypotheses illustrate their biological rationale and subsequent literature support where available. These findings support temporal guidance in semantic space as a scalable mechanism for proposing biomedical hypotheses for subsequent scientific evaluation.

In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.

Real-world learning scenarios often exhibit asymmetries between training and inference, where additional or higher-quality information is available only during training. The Learning Under Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm provides a formal framework to study such settings. Despite research interest over the years, the extensive literature on LUPI remains highly fragmented. In this survey, we present a comprehensive and structured overview of research on LUPI and its related formulations. We review 107 papers published between 2009 and 2025 and propose a novel unified taxonomy based on two core dimensions: the underlying machine learning models, spanning both shallow and deep architectures, and the methodological strategies used to integrate privileged information. Additionally, we provide an extensive overview of the various application domains and the particular types of privileged modalities used. We also discuss key insights and open challenges, focusing on how and when privileged information can be effectively leveraged in modern machine learning systems.

Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.

The relevance of this study is determined by the fact that, for Level 4 autonomous ships, traditional situational awareness architectures do not comply with Rule 5 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea concerning continuous lookout by all available means, since such ships do not distinguish between random noise, sensor degradation, and cyberattacks. This paper proposes a Level 1 situational awareness architecture consistent with the Endsley model. Sensors are divided into a continuously active core (radar, satellite navigation systems, Automatic Identification System, optical and thermal imaging cameras, microphones, and other systems) and specialized modules (LiDAR, Doppler speed log, sonar). A Sensor Trust Manager with a quality metric and a trust management protocol for navigational information sensors have been developed, combining noise level, deviation from the predicted value, cyberattack (spoofing) detection, and packet loss. The Trust Manager operates a six-state automaton (NOMINAL, DEGRADED, SUSPECT, ISOLATED, RECOVERING, FAILED) with transition hysteresis, ensuring resistance to short-term interference without false sensor isolation. Trust Managers ensure the isolation of unreliable sources before data enter the fusion filters. Thus, only physically reliable and time-consistent data are supplied to complex fusion algorithms (Kalman filters, trackers), which is critical for preventing “contamination” of the target vessel state assessment. The proposed architecture combines compliance with Rule 5, scenario adaptation through the division of sensors into basic and specialized groups, and cyber resilience (spoofing) through signal evaluation based on quality criteria, creating a theoretical basis for certification of Level 4 autonomous marine surface ships in accordance with the requirements of the Code of Safety for Autonomous Surface Ships .

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has driven the development of diverse educational technologies. In this context, Artificial Intelligence-based Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems (AI-based MALS) have emerged as an efficient alternative to complement the teaching and learning process. However, the advancement of these systems is hindered by significant challenges such as insufficient software architectural support, lack of standardization, and inadequate requirements coverage and correctness. Addressing these challenges requires designing high-quality software architectures. Accordingly, research focused on the design, development, and evaluation of software architectures for AI-based MALS is critical from a software engineering standpoint. Although some secondary studies have explored related topics through literature reviews and systematic mapping, no comprehensive secondary review has identified the principal architectural aspects of AI-based MALS design. This study conducts a Literature Review (LR) of software architectures that integrate Artificial Intelligence into Mobile Adaptive Learning Systems. The main objective is to identify and compare the critical aspects of software architectures for proposed AI-based MALS in the specialized literature. The findings highlight several essential elements that software architectures for AI-based MALS should address, including requirements, quality attributes, stakeholders, user services, architectural views and styles, components, and implementation technologies. The primary finding of this study is the absence of a reference software architecture in the reviewed studies that comprehensively addresses the requirements needed to develop AI-based MALS to support adaptive learning in mobile distributed environments.

documents.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) trajectory planning in dense urban environments requires models that generalize to rare or previously unseen scenario types. Deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on large datasets perform poorly in such data-scarce conditions, while large language models (LLMs) generalize well but lack the numerical precision required for low-level vehicle control. This paper presents a hybrid trajectory planning framework that fuses a finetuned LLM with a multi-branch DNN at the trajectory level and applies a Model Predictive Control (MPC) controller as a final optimization stage. Gemini 1.5 Flash, fine-tuned on 479 labeled scenario-trajectory pairs, generates 15- aypoint trajectory proposals from structured textual scene descriptions. A modular DNN processes the same scene as a numerical input vector and produces a parallel trajectory proposal. The two proposals are fused by a learned trajectory refinement network, and the output is passed to an MPC controller that enforces vehicle dynamics constraints while minimizing a multi-objective cost function. Training relies on a three-step distortion- based augmentation technique, curve distortion, scale distortion, and Gaussian smoothing, that generates semi-realistic trajectory variants from a base dataset of over 70,000 labeled rows, reducing the data volume required for effective DNN training. Evaluation across 200 runs in the CARLA simulator on unseen urban scenarios shows that the MPC-enhanced hybrid model achieves an Average Displacement Error (ADE) of 0.66 m and a Final Displacement Error (FDE) of 1.94 m, corresponding to improvements of 37.7% and 34.3% over the DNN-only baseline. The collision rate (CR) decreases from 3.71% to 2.90%, a 21.8% reduction. These results establish that trajectory-level fusion of LLM semantic reasoning with DNN-based feature extraction delivers measurable accuracy and safety gains in data-efficient autonomous driving conditions. The ADE/FDE improvements are statistically significant (p < 0.001). The collision-rate reduction is a consistent trend across ablations, but it is not statistically significant at n = 200 runs (see Section 4.4).

ABSTRACT Identity‐based Recommendation (IDR) plays a crucial role in modern personalized recommendation systems by leveraging users' identity information and historical interactions to model long‐term user preferences. However, existing IDR methods face three critical challenges: difficulty in fully capturing latent user preference, limited representational capacity, and poor adaptability to cold‐start scenarios. To address these issues, we propose the LLM‐Enhanced Semantic Information Alignment for ID Recommendation (ESIA‐IDR) framework, which systematically integrates semantic features generated by large language models (LLMs) into ID‐based recommendation. ESIA‐IDR first employs LLMs to deeply perceive unstructured textual data, such as user reviews and product descriptions, thereby effectively mining users' latent interest patterns. An independent pretraining mechanism is then applied to optimize the training dynamics of semantic and ID embeddings, mitigating inconsistencies in convergence behavior. Additionally, a feature discretization strategy is adopted to enhance semantic feature compatibility with traditional recommendation pipelines. During the recommendation phase, semantic‐enhanced features and collaborative signals are jointly modeled to achieve robust performance in cold‐start environments. ESIA‐IDR consists of four key components: Semantic and Interest Perception, Semantic Alignment, Discrete Feature Construction, and Recommendation Integration. By combining pretraining, dimensionality reduction, and similarity‐based bucketing, the framework achieves effective alignment between semantic features and ID feature spaces, bridging the semantic‐structural gap and improving user preference modeling accuracy. Extensive experiments on multiple real‐world datasets demonstrate that ESIA‐IDR achieves a 2.21% improvement in NDCG and a 1.48% improvement in Hit Rate compared to the best‐performing baselines, validating its effectiveness in enhancing recommendation performance.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly reshaping the landscape of data-driven research discovery, offering unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding, knowledge synthesis, and intelligent query resolution. This chapter explores the transformative role of LLMs within next-generation research infrastructures, examining how these models augment traditional data pipelines, accelerate hypothesis generation, and enable cross-domain knowledge integration. A proposed methodology integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), domain-adaptive fine-tuning, and semantic indexing is presented and evaluated on multi-disciplinary research corpora. Experimental results demonstrate significant gains in retrieval accuracy, citation relevance, and researcher productivity. The chapter further discusses practical advantages, persistent challenges including hallucination and bias, and a forward-looking perspective on human-AI collaborative research ecosystems.

Academic writing is non-linear, iterative, and structure-driven, requiring authors to develop fragmented ideas into arguments with local coherence and global consistency. However, current AI-assisted tools primarily exchange linear prompts and free-form text, forcing authors to reconstruct generated logic and repeatedly verify its alignment with their structural intentions. We propose object-oriented writing (OOW), an OOD-inspired representation and interaction paradigm in which persistent writing objects serve as shared, manipulable referents for authors and AI. We instantiate OOW in LogicTree, an Overleaf-integrated prototype that combines a hierarchical object representation with a structure-grounded writing assistance module for author-initiated generation and issue-grounded revision and a structural logical review module for inspecting local coherence and global consistency. A within-subjects study (N=12) provides initial evidence that, in controlled academic writing tasks, LogicTree helps users structure ideas, reduces workload, and improves measured logical quality compared with a conversational baseline.

Long COVID syndrome represents a significant public health concern, with healthcare workers constituting a population at particularly high risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequent persistent symptoms. To evaluate the prevalence of Long COVID syndrome in healthcare employees of IRCCS Policlinico San Matteo Foundation over a four-year time window from the pandemic onset. An anonymous survey was conducted among healthcare workers with documented SARS-CoV-2 infection since February 2020. Long COVID syndrome was defined as persistent symptoms lasting beyond 12 weeks from the acute infection, extending to 12 months or more. The Fisher exact test and the McNemar test were used to compare prevalences between groups and over time, respectively. Unsupervised learning techniques were used for identifying patient aggregation. Among 771 respondents (response rate 41.41% of employees with previous SARS-CoV-2 infection), the overall Long COVID syndrome cumulative prevalence (participants experiencing symptoms at any time point) was 27.9% (215/771; 95% CI: 24.7–31.2%), with point prevalence decreasing over time: 26.0% (95% CI 23.0–29.0%) at 3 months, 20.0% (95% CI 17.0–23.0%) at 6 months, and 16.0% (95% CI 14.0–19.0%) at 12 months post-infection. Significant associations were found with job position ( p = 0.004), with nurses showing the highest prevalence (35.0%). Fatigue, joint and muscle pain, concentration troubles, and memory difficulties emerged as the most persistent symptoms over time. Long COVID syndrome affects more than one-quarter of healthcare workers with previous SARS-CoV-2 infection, with symptom persistence demonstrating a gradual decline over time. These findings have important implications for occupational health management and workforce planning in healthcare settings.

Abstract Reliable prediction of plant growth and physiological characteristics can aid effective phenotyping and computational evaluation of environmental treatments. The purpose of this study was to create a leakage-controlled machine learning system to predict the endpoint characteristics of rice seedlings under controlled electromagnetic field (EMF) conditions with early longitudinal measurements. Two data sets were analyzed, one synthetic and the other generated in the computer, consisting of the 2800 observations of 200 plants randomly distributed from control and low, medium and high-EMF exposure groups respectively. The morphological, biomass, chlorophyll, leaf-area and image-derived phenotypic variables were summarized into longitudinal features for Days 3–7 and Day-14 measurements were only used as prediction endpoints. Plant-level grouped training, validation and independent testing sets with a ratio of 70:15:15 were adopted so as to reduce the amount of information leaked from repeated measurements taken from individual plants. Three models were tested for predicting final height, dry biomass and chlorophyll content: Random Forest, Bagged Ensemble and Gaussian Process Regression. The models had an R² of 0.9645, 0.9698 and 0.6676 for the synthetic data set, and 0.9051, 0.9202 and 0.8194 for the computational data set. Independent-test RMSE values ranged from 0.1783–0.00421 cm/g for the synthetic dataset and 0.3298–0.00915 cm/g and 1.1339 for the computational data based on the predicted trait. In general, early longitudinal phenotypes showed promise for computational prediction of rice seedling endpoints and model performance depended on trait and data generation structure. The framework offers a repeatable method for the prediction and comparison of leakage-controlled rice phenotypic reactions using controlled EMF exposure.

Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

Under the background of the "Healthy China" initiative and the continuous improvement of the occupational health system, pneumoconiosis still poses a challenge to the health rights and interests of workers and the ability of public governance. This disease has the characteristics of long incubation period, irreversible course, and difficult traceability of responsibility. This article reviews the experience of the United States and other developed countries in the control of pneumoconiosis, and uses the panel data of 31 provincial administrative units in China from 2007 to 2023 to construct a two-way fixed effect model. Given data limitations, the reported incidence rate of tuberculosis is used as a proxy indicator to examine macro-level factors such as industrial structure, industrial pollution, public services, labor protection, and medical resources. The study also analyzes institutional inflection points in China’s governance of pneumoconiosis by combining policy documents with prosecutorial case studies. The study found that the share of the secondary sector and sulfur dioxide emissions is significantly and positively correlated with reported incidence rates, while the share of healthcare expenditure, urbanization rates, and infrastructure are significantly and negatively correlated. The relationship between the number of workers covered by work-related injury insurance, the allocation of healthcare professionals, and human capital lacks stability. Case studies further indicate that the coordination among workplace protection, occupational health records, occupational disease diagnosis, work-related injury determination, and benefit payments is a key institutional condition affecting the prevention of pneumoconiosis and the protection of patients. Based on these findings, this paper proposes that the development of the pneumoconiosis management system for the 15th Five-Year Plan should strengthen dust control at the source, protection for high-risk populations, grassroots occupational health services, cross-regional information coordination, and long-term collaborative care, thereby promoting the coordinated development of occupational health risk prevention and control and the protection of workers’ rights.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability among older adults and is increasingly recognized as a significant occupational health issue, especially among healthcare workers who are frequently exposed to repetitive knee strain. This study aims to identify the burden of primary knee osteoarthritis (KOA) among healthcare workers at a tertiary care institution in Bangladesh. Objective: The present study aimed to assess the magnitude and associated factors of primary knee osteoarthritis (KOA) among healthcare workers at BMU. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional study included 185 healthcare workers selected by simple random sampling at BMU. Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) was diagnosed using the 2016 ACR clinical criteria. Data were collected using a modified and Bangla-adapted COPCORD questionnaire, including PHQ-9 and B-HAQ-DI tools. Anthropometric measurements were taken to calculate BMI. Data were analyzed using SPSS v23.0 with appropriate statistical tests; a p-value <0.05 was considered significant. Results: Among 185 healthcare workers, 42.2% were diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis (KOA), and 40% had a B-HAQ-DI score ≥0.8, indicating functional disability. Most KOA cases (57.7%) were female, and mild disability was the most common severity (28.9%). KOA prevalence was similar across physicians (40.5%), nurses (43.1%), and supporting staff (44%). Age was significantly associated with KOA (p = 0.034), with the highest prevalence in the 41–50 age group. Logistic regression identified increasing age (OR 1.064, p = 0.003) and female sex (OR 2.153, p = 0.020) as independent predictors. Conclusion: Knee osteoarthritis was prevalent among healthcare workers, with age and female sex as key predictors, highlighting the need for early intervention and preventive strategies in this population J Dhaka National Med. Peer code review is widely used in programming and software engineering education, but its instructional value depends on the quality of student feedback rather than review completion alone. In large classes, instructors can readily monitor participation but lack scalable methods for assessing whether feedback is relevant, concrete, and constructive, limiting opportunities for timely instructional intervention. To address this gap, this study developed and evaluated the Review Engagement Graph (REG), an instructor focused learning analytics dashboard that integrates multilabel artificial intelligence classification of feedback quality with interactive network visualization. REG operationalizes feedback quality across three independent dimensions and translates five recurring visual patterns into corresponding pedagogical actions while preserving instructor judgment. The system was evaluated in two studies. Study 1 compared seven classification models spanning traditional machine learning, deep learning, fine-tuned transformers, and prompted large language models using 2,398 peer review comments independently annotated by two experts. Fine-tuned RoBERTa achieved the strongest overall performance, with a macro F1 score of 0.828. Study 2 evaluated REG with instructors and teaching assistants through scenario-based sessions. REG achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 81.13, exceeding the benchmark of 68, and a mean perceived usefulness score of 4.31 out of 5. These findings demonstrate that AI classified feedback quality indicators can be transformed into actionable visual evidence through a pattern to action framework that supports timely and informed instructor decision making.

Self-improving LLM agents edit their own harness, the prompts and rules around a fixed model, and keep an edit only if an acceptance gate scores it higher on a batch of tasks. Such a gate sees what the harness does under the current model, not what it would still prevent if one safeguard failed. When safeguards overlap, deleting one is masked: the others still block the harm, so the gate decides on task success alone and redundancy erodes unseen. We measure harm for every subset of four written safeguards in two agent environments and run 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules, mostly as controlled deletion experiments, plus three runs of the GEPA optimizer. A deletion behind another working safeguard adds almost no observable harm. A paired significance test blocks deletions that pass by chance but not deletions that genuinely raise task success, and a larger evaluation batch lets it delete cheaper safeguards: at the same cost, 20-task batches kept every harness protected while 40-task batches lost all six. Large harm audits prevent exposure but not the loss of depth, which turns into harm when the harness is reused with a weaker model. GEPA kept every safety rule verbatim, yet two of its three final harnesses misused credentials under a weaker model. A statistical model frozen before the runs predicts where each gate's protection breaks as safeguard cost and batch size change, and freezing safety text or auditing one-layer ablations preserves depth.

documents.abstract: Search and rescue is a team operation where uncertainty and hazards can fracture coordination and safety. Integrative stacks fusing information systems, UAVs, and robots can rebuild situational awareness and reduce exposure, but they are mostly passive. AI agents now show emergent goal pursuit through planning, self-correction, and replanning from noisy observations. It is unclear whether a human digital twin communicates interpersonally like a human under the same role-bounded information constraints. In this paper, we compare humans and HDTs in a role-conditioned, attribute-matched search and rescue simulation, quantifying nine-category responses for Engineer, Medic, and Transporter roles. We find distinct role-driven interaction signatures and a consistent human–HDT shift, with fewer questions and explicit agreements, offset by role-specific neutral stability and socioemotional support. The implication is that HDTs should better balance support with questioning and agreeing behaviors that humans rely on to confirm shared understanding and reach decisions in search and rescue.

Digital transformation in the world of education requires teachers to be able to adapt to technological developments while developing learning that is creative, innovative, and in accordance with the needs of students. This community service activity aims to improve teachers' competence in utilizing digital technology as a medium and learning resource and encourage the creation of more interactive and student-centered learning. Activities are carried out through socialization, training, direct practice, discussion, and mentoring. Activity materials include the use of digital platforms and applications for learning, the development of interactive learning media, the wise use of artificial intelligence (AI), and strategies for designing digital-based creative learning activities. The results of the activity show an increase in teachers' understanding and skills in selecting, using, and developing digital technology to support the learning process. Teachers are also able to produce more interesting, interactive, and contextual media designs and learning activities. This activity shows that digital transformation is not only related to mastery of technology, but also to teachers' ability to integrate technology, pedagogy, and creativity to create meaningful learning experiences. Thus, strengthening teachers' digital competencies needs to be carried out in a sustainable manner so that teachers are able to become creative, adaptive, and innovative educators in facing educational changes in the digital era.

Abstract Background: Large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve patient data, invoke clinical tools and execute multi-step tasks inside electronic health record (EHR) systems. Authenticating an agent session does not establish that each subsequent action is consistent with the clinician’s purpose, the assigned patient or the agent’s delegated authority. Objectives: We study continuous, purpose-aware authorization of individual clinical-agent actions, and test whether temporal graph structure and explicit patient and purpose context improve detection of unauthorized actions over event-level, sequential and static graph models. Methods: We propose MedTrustGraph, which represents clinicians, agents, patients, tools, FHIR resources and clinical purposes as typed nodes connected by timestamped interactions. A graph attention encoder produces event embeddings that a causal gated recurrent unit processes in temporal order; patient-scope and purpose-scope checks supply Zero-Trust context; and a Platt-calibrated risk estimate is mapped to ALLOW, VERIFY or DENY by a deterministic policy engine that retains final authority. We built a synthetic FHIR-style benchmark modelled on MedAgentBench with 5,000 agent trajectories and 36,855 access events (8,448 unauthorized) spanning cross-patient access, purpose drift, privilege escalation and bulk record retrieval, evaluated on a chronological trajectory-level 70/15/15 split. Results: Using only leakage-safe observable features, the temporal graph model reached F1 =0.8905, AUROC =0.9767 and AUPRC =0.9517, versus F1 =0.8062 for XGBoost and 0.7918 for a static graph attention network. In a controlled ablation configuration the full model reached F1 =0.9653 (95% CI 0.9544–0.9741); removing patient context, purpose context, graph structure or temporal structure lowered F1 by 0.2173, 0.0200, 0.0188 and 0.0174 (all Holm-adjusted p<10 −4 ). Shuffling event order lowered F1 to 0.8279, while removing 30% of edges changed it by under 0.002. The calibrated policy layer allowed 0 of 652 unauthorized events (95% CI 0–0.59%) and auto-allowed 98.64% of authorized events with a 1.90% verification workload. The code and data are available at https://github.com/Kamrul01685/MedTrustGraph. Conclusions: On this benchmark, temporal order and patient/purpose context carry authorization signal beyond event-level and static-graph models, and separating learned risk from deterministic policy yields a low-workload decision layer. Because benchmark labels were generated from patient- and purpose-scope rules, context-augmented scores are upper bounds; validation on real or independently generated agent traces is required.

The human brain, and large language models, must retain, integrate and access huge quantities of information. The retained information depends upon the details of the encoding. The integration depends on elaborate connectivity. The access depends on a relationship to the entire database that includes the meanings and encoded information. The irreducible tension between the micro details of encoding information, and the total database perspective required for meaning, can be resolved only by an analytic tool, like the informational entropy of all or part of the data. Reified quantum mechanics, with a mechanism to resolve indeterminacy, can be viewed as a model of Panpsychism (Remler, 2026a) with the necessary analytic tools. This model provides a rational framework to understand evolution, with the rising centrality of negative entropy, and the massive encephalization manifest in human beings. The result is a scientifically based, conceptual model of the high-level human brain function including Consciousness and the range of Subjectivity.

Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the cognitive conditions of knowledge innovation. While human–AI collaboration improves the efficiency of knowledge production, it may also induce creators to outsourcing cognitive work to AI systems. This study conceptualized this tendency as task-level metacognitive disengagement, defined as the immediate reduction of planning, monitoring, and reflection within a specific AI-assisted task, and, drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory, examined its impact on knowledge innovation quality, its psychological mechanism, and boundary conditions through four complementary experiments. Experiment 1 showed that higher AI assistance significantly increased metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 2 revealed that cognitive offloading partially mediated the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 3 confirmed the negative effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality, specifically on novelty, usefulness, and developability, with metacognitive disengagement partially mediating this effect. Experiment 4 tested the proposed moderated mediation model and found that task complexity strengthened, whereas individual AI literacy weakened, the negative indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. These findings reveal a hidden cognitive cost behind the efficiency gains of human–AI collaboration and provide empirical evidence and theoretical implications for cultivating innovative talent and designing human–AI collaborative mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

This chapter examines how machine learning is transforming metadata automation and enrichment across research infrastructures, libraries, and data repositories. Synthesizing natural language processing, computer vision, large language models, and knowledge graph approaches, it analyzes how automated subject indexing, entity extraction, image captioning, author disambiguation, schema crosswalks, and ontology learning address persistent metadata quality deficits at scale. A machine learning enrichment pipeline model and a taxonomy of ML approaches are introduced, alongside a comparative modality table and performance bubble chart. The chapter critically examines FAIR data alignment, ethical governance, and implementation barriers.

Abstract. Here, we present and update a research agenda on mobile-first and responsive cartographic design published in the Journal of Location Based Services in 2024. We first introduce our collective process within the ICA (International Cartographic Association) to develop a set of three research agendas articles on mobile cartography that span user issues, technology issues, and design issues related to mobile maps and visualizations. We then describe a partial design space and 20 related research challenges from our assigned perspective of mobile map and visualization design. We then employ the 2024 research agenda as an analytical framework to review recent literature and reflect on emerging challenges and opportunities for research and development on mobile cartography given the fast-paced innovations in GeoAI (Geospatial Artificial Intelligence) since 2024. We conclude with priority considerations for integrating mobile cartography and GeoAI.

ABSTRACT The shipping industry plays a vital role in global trade and also exerts significant environmental and social pressures due to high fuel consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and intensive port activities. Implementing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices offers a strategic pathway to enhance sustainability performance in this sector; however, it remains difficult to determine which managerial and operational actions can most effectively drive improvements in ESG performance. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates a large language model (LLM), an extended q‐ rung orthopair fuzzy rough set ( q‐ ROFRS)‐based Delphi‐weighted influence nonlinear gauge system (WINGS) model, and a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) simulation. This approach systematically identifies critical success factors (CSFs), analyzes their cause–effect relationships, and simulates their dynamic influence on ESG performance in the shipping industry. The findings reveal that six CSFs, including structured board oversight, global policy engagement, comprehensive legal compliance framework, employee‐centric culture, effective communication strategy, and integrated water resource management, serve as key causal drivers within the ESG system. FCM‐based scenario simulations suggest that full activation of these modeled drivers could substantially improve projected ESG performance under the assumed scenario conditions. This research offers a dual contribution: Theoretically, it extends fuzzy decision‐making and AI‐driven causal modeling to complex sustainability systems; practically, it provides actionable guidance for shipping companies and policymakers to strengthen ESG integration, meet the International Maritime Organization's net‐zero targets, and advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

This study aimed to develop a causal relationship model and identify the direct and indirect effects of situational awareness on some basic futsal skills among fourth-year students at the College of Physical Education and Sports Sciences, Al-Qadisiyah University during the academic year 2025–2026. The research problem stemmed from observing student training sessions, revealing a significant disparity in cognitive abilities and skill-based decision-making despite their similar technical levels. The researcher employed a descriptive methodology using both survey and correlational approaches. The research population consisted of 100 students randomly selected and divided into construction pilot (20 students) and application (60 students) samples. A 14-item situational awareness scale was adapted for the sports context and its validity and reliability were verified (the corrected split-half reliability coefficient was 0.819 and Cronbach's Alpha was 0.866). The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) and AMOS software (v.24) were used to analyze the data. The results showed that students possessed a high level of situational awareness with a mean score of 33.090 and a standard deviation of 4.856. The study recommended incorporating the causal model into educational and training curricula to link cognitive-psychological factors with technical skill performance in futsal.

Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) offer an effective approach for solving complex and large-scale problems in distributed artificial intelligence by dividing them into smaller subtasks handled by multiple autonomous agents. Each agent can perceive its environment, process information, make decisions, and perform actions according to its assigned objectives. Agents communicate, collaborate, and coordinate to achieve individual and collective goals, providing advantages such as scalability, adaptability, flexibility, robustness, and fault tolerance. The proposed Multi-Agent Task Automation System uses heterogeneous agents dynamically assigned tasks according to their capabilities, resource availability, current workload, task priority, execution cost, and contextual relevance. A mediator-based coordination mechanism supports agent discovery and task routing while allowing direct peer-to-peer communication when necessary. Dynamic task allocation and load balancing help distribute work efficiently. Reinforcement learning can enhance agent decision-making by allowing agents to learn from feedback and improve their strategies over time. The system also incorporates fault detection, recovery, authentication, secure communication, and trust evaluation to improve reliability and security. The implementation uses Python, AutoGen, large language models, APIs, and external tools, with structured message passing enabling agents to interact and execute tasks collaboratively. Tasks are initiated through user input and processed using iterative communication, reasoning, and tool execution. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of MAS to improve task execution efficiency, response time, resource utilization, adaptability, scalability, and fault tolerance compared with traditional centralized approaches. However, communication overhead, coordination complexity, security risks, synchronization, and efficient task allocation remain important challenges.

This chapter highlights the evolution of digital twins from passive data repositories to intelligent systems capable of contextual reasoning, supporting informed decision-making. We introduce the multi-aspect digital twin named MADT4BC, a core DYNABIC component designed to address the observability challenge and increase situational awareness in multi-scale critical infrastructures through AI-based assisting technology. MADT4BC reads and stores heterogeneous data streams from the physical infrastructure, connecting these to a semantically rich digital representation of real infrastructure using knowledge graphs. In response to user requests, AI agents are deployed to operate on top of the knowledge graph: creating, extracting, contextualizing, and reasoning over the collected operational data and the asset information to provide timely responses. We validate MADT4BC through one real-world use case, showcasing both knowledge creation and extraction abilities.

Background: Social media is a critical channel of real-time information channel during natural disasters, but the informal and fragmented nature of tweets makes automatic classification difficult. Named entity recognition (NER) can capture contextual cues, such as affected locations. However, how entity information should be incorporated into classifiers and its value for disaster mapping remain underexplored. Objective: This study investigates whether NER can improve disaster-tweet classification and support clustering-based disaster mapping for humanitarian decision support. Methods: Eight configurations were evaluated using raw text: linear and BiLSTM classification heads combined with three input representations (Raw, Inline Tag, and Special Token), and two architecture-level injection models (BiLSTM+TagEmb and Two-Stream) using raw text. An ablation study compared eight pretrained language models across four architectures and input variants. In addition, six density-based clustering algorithms were applied to NER-extracted location entities to map the spatial distribution of disaster events. Results: The two-stream model achieved the highest performance (macro F1 = 0.947), followed by the BiLSTM classifier with raw input (0.914), indicating that the architecture-level entity integration outperforms the input-level entity marking. VDBSCAN, HDBSCAN, and OPTICS produced the most cohesive clusters (silhouette > 0.97). Conclusion: Integrating entity information at the architectural level is more effective than embedding entity markers in the input text. Density-based clustering is better suited to the exploratory discovery of spatial patterns than to reproducing predefined categories. These findings provide practical guidance for designing disaster-tweet classifiers and selecting unsupervised methods to analyze disaster-related social media data. Although the proposed approach may contribute to situational awareness, its utility for operational humanitarian decision-making remains to be empirically validated. Keywords: Disaster tweet classification, Named entity recognition, natural language processing, social media analytics, disaster

"Munzur University’s Rare Earth Elements (REE) Operational Program addresses Türkiye’s R&D, product development, education, capacity-building, and regional development objectives in the fields of strategic raw materials and advanced technology applications through a holistic approach. Within the scope of Munzur University’s regional development-oriented mission differentiation, its area of specialization has been defined as “Strategic Raw Materials and Advanced Technology Applications.” Accordingly, rare earth elements, critical minerals, advanced materials, recycling, chemical purification, environmentally friendly production, and the development of high valueadded technological products have become priority areas of work. The project titled “Enhancing the Research and Innovation Capacity of Türkiye in Rare Earth Elements,” co-financed by the European Union and the Republic of Türkiye, aims to contribute to the establishment of a sustainable REE supply chain in Türkiye. The final beneficiary of the project is the General Directorate of Industry (SGM), while its partners are Munzur University Rare Earth Elements Application and Research Center (MUNTEAM) and the General Directorate of Mineral Research and Exploration (MTA). Within the scope of the project, the MUNTEAM building was allocated, laboratory infrastructure was established, research partnerships were developed, and the center began carrying out activities in analysis, accreditation, education, R&D, product development, and business development. The current status of the program is not limited solely to the establishment of laboratory infrastructure. Projects supported by The Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK), the Presidency of Strategy and Budget, and collaborations with various universities cover a wide range of fields, including ore enrichment, chemical purification, solvent extraction, bioleaching, recycling, advanced alloys, optoelectronic materials, catalysts, biomedical applications, and data analytics. In addition, training programs for R&D professionals, the critical minerals optimization team, and data science and artificial intelligence-based analytical approaches strengthen the program’s human resource capacity and methodological competence. As a result, Munzur University’s REE Operational Program holds a strategic position in terms of Türkiye’s critical mineral independence, green transition, defense industry, e-mobility, digital technologies, and circular economy objectives. Internationalization, accreditation, open innovation, industrial integration, and the establishment of new graduate programs and institutes are of critical importance for the sustainability of the program."

Against rising graduate employment pressure and the widespread application of digital technology across industries, the curriculum of higher vocational Traditional Chinese Pharmacy (TCP) fails to fully match the competency requirements of actual jobs. This research intends to quantitatively analyze the correlation between students’ course scores and employment performance, offering data support for curriculum revision and optimization in vocational colleges. Using data from 236 TCP graduates, the study classified employment destinations into six types and converted them into binary employment variables. Mutual Information (MI) was employed to quantify the nonlinear correlation between 49 course scores and employment results. Combined with a Monte Carlo-assisted elimination algorithm, the research filtered out courses with no statistical connection to employment. Repeated random sampling ensured stable numerical results and course rankings. The findings show that core TCP professional courses do not occupy leading positions in the MI ranking. Sensitivity tests by removing average grades further verified the reliability of the conclusions. This study proves MI is a valid tool for exploring links between courses and employment, while pointing out its limitation: MI only reflects correlation instead of causality. It is recommended that curriculum teams refer to MI rankings, align course design with talent training goals and industry needs, and add digital competency courses including artificial intelligence and big data analysis to adapt to industrial upgrading.

Background Cumulative exposure to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) is associated with an increased risk of substance use, overdose, and suicide. Rural children are more likely to experience most ACEs. There is limited literature contextualizing rural individuals’ experiences with ACEs. Public Health 3.0 calls for multisector partner engagement to generate collective impact. The purpose of this study was to evaluate rural providers’ perspectives on challenges and recommendations for ACEs mitigation in their community from a cross-sector context. Participants and setting Participants were 74 providers enrolled in an online ACEs training. Participants lived and/or worked in five rural Missouri counties with high drug overdose death rates. Methods This was a conventional content analysis of written responses to structured discussion prompts from three training modules. Analysis included familiarization, inductive identification of major codes, and refinement of codes, followed by independent coding by two authors until consensus, and reporting major patterns. Artificial intelligence supported preliminary code development. An adapted Sequential Intercept Model (SIM) framework organized challenges and recommendations by setting. Results Results included personal stories about how ACEs impacted their communities through overdose, suicide, homelessness, unemployment, and adverse health effects. Settings included schools, government, healthcare, daycares, criminal justice, Extension, fire departments, libraries, and nonprofits. Participants recommended expanding the ACEs definition to include satanic abuse, bullying, incest, war, genocide, military family stressors, and death of a loved one. Intervention recommendations included whole-family interventions, community-wide training, trauma-informed training, expanded access to treatment, classes in prison/jails, and fostering positive childhood experiences. Conclusion Community voice is necessary to contextualize setting-specific insights that inform development of upstream interventions appropriate for and tailored to the community. Participants identified both strategies that could be incorporated into everyday practice—including empathy, listening, providing judgment-free and safe spaces, providing food for children experiencing hunger, encouraging positive childhood experiences, mentoring, and connecting individuals with resources for food, shelter, clothing, and mental health—and broader structural changes that may require policy-level action. The adapted SIM organizes these concepts.

While federal reform movements have shaped modern public education through legislation, education has also been subject to dramatic social, political, and technological pressures. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic forced schools to adapt to distance learning within days to weeks. Virtual schooling came with benefits as well as challenges. When in-person instruction resumed, many classrooms were far more reliant on technology than they had been prior to the pandemic. Similarly, the widespread adoption of generative AI technology, beginning in 2022, has had both positive and negative consequences for education. Throughout these massive social and technological shifts, new political debates in education have become prominent. Schools are facing political pressure at the local and state levels, financial pressure from the popularization of vouchers, and social pressure from backlash against Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion measures. This chapter describes the current social, technological, and political environments which future-thinking leaders must respond.

Introduction: Night vision goggles (NVGs) extend the capability of helicopter crews to conduct night operations, but they do not reproduce daytime vision and may alter the visual conditions in which spatial disorientation (SD) develops. A historical helicopter study reported an approximately five-fold higher SD-related accident rate during night-vision device (NVD) operations than during daytime flight. This review examines how NVG/an night vision imaging system characteristics, degraded visual environments (DVE) and crew-system interactions may contribute to the development or delayed recognition of SD, and identifies practical safety barriers for helicopter operations. Method: This purposive narrative review integrates peer-reviewed aviation-medicine and human-factors literature with a structured analysis of seven publicly documented helicopter accidents or serious incidents involving NVG/NVD operations. The case analysis distinguishes official investigation findings from the author’s interpretation and maps case evidence onto recurrent perceptual, cognitive and operational mechanisms. Results: Across the seven cases, recurrent patterns involved low-contrast or featureless scenes, loss or degradation of visual references, blooming or incompatible lighting, delayed transition to instruments and attentional or crew-monitoring failures. Five proposed conceptual operational pathways summarise how these conditions may converge on SD. Conclusions: The principal hazard is not NVG use per se, but continued reliance on a partially reliable external image that may omit a stable horizon, surface texture, optical flow or valid depth cues. Mitigation therefore depends on predefined visual-reference minima and abort criteria, early transition to instruments, compatible lighting, radar-altimeter and flight-parameter monitoring, realistic DVE training, and assertive crew coordination.

documents.abstract: Objective: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as guideline-decision support in oncology, but most validation has occurred in common cancers, where clinicians can usually recognize errors. The safety-critical setting is the opposite — rare cancers, where local expertise is limited, and errors may go unrecognized. Whether common-cancer concordance reflects the reliability needed there is unclear. Methods: We benchmarked GPT-5.2 against the EAU-ASCO 2025 Penile Cancer Guidelines using 100 guideline-derived questions across five domains and three zero-shot prompting strategies, yielding 300 responses. Two experienced urologists, blinded to prompt identity, scored concordance on a 3-point scale and classified errors as hallucination, omission, temporal, or reasoning. The primary analysis was a mixed-effects ordinal logistic regression with question as a random intercept; a cluster-robust logistic regression served as sensitivity. Reporting followed TRIPOD-LLM. Results: GPT-5.2 was fully concordant in 236 of 300 responses (78.7%; 95% confidence interval, 73.7–82.9; weighted κ=0.914). Prompt strategy did not improve performance (role-play +3 percentage points; 95% credible interval, −2 to +9). The domain effect was not robust once between-question clustering was modeled. Among 64 non-concordant responses, omission predominated (47.7%) and reasoning errors followed (37.5%); in treatment, omission accounted for 68.0% of errors, including loss of guideline-specified detail. Four questions were uniformly discordant across all three prompts. Conclusion: Headline concordance overstated clinical reliability. The clinically informative finding was not the overall accuracy but the structure of failure — omission of decision-critical treatment detail and stable errors. Prompt engineering did not rescue performance. Current LLM output may assist orientation in rare-cancer decision pathways but is not ready as stand-alone guideline-decision support.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) often operates under sequential task exposure, uneven compute, and decentralized coordination. Here, we present a cancer-inspired, or oncomorphic, multi-agent framework in which simulated neural agents can replicate, mutate their neural network architecture, migrate across task environments, undergo ecological turnover, and recruit learning/ecological resources from a finite shared reserve. We evaluate the framework in controlled synthetic nonlinear classification environments in which each agent trains only on its local task, allowing population ecology rather than centralized optimization to determine which neural network architectures persist. For various initial conditions, we find that stronger selection increased the endpoint local accuracy of surviving agent populations. Architecture mutation played a state-dependent role: diverse initial populations performed best at low mutation, whereas clonal large-architecture populations benefited from mutation-generated variation. Selection also increased end-of-run multi-task competence, measured by evaluating surviving agents on all environments without additional training. Recruitment and elevated baseline replication reshaped demographic support while prediction quality remained within a narrow band, consistent with redistribution of finite learning resources. Time-resolved entropy and dominance analyses revealed concentration toward successful architectures, while finite training cycles kept agents in a non-asymptotic learning regime. These results provide proof-of-concept mechanistic evidence that oncomorphic population dynamics may offer a route to decentralized adaptation in engineering applications under bounded local resources.

A foundation model trained on over 40 million face photographs can now estimate biological age and predict the survival of cancer patients from a single photograph. Today the photograph is taken once and the model gives one survival score, with no sign of how firm that score is. This concept note describes a simple check that can sit on top of such a model. From the photograph that is already stored, the computer makes two to four versions by changing only the photograph's own processing settings, within the range the camera, the capture software and the clinic permit. The same model reads every version, unchanged. If the survival scores stay together, the prediction is firm. If they spread out, it depends on a setting. One number, the spread value, shows which case it is. A computer-decided shunting action then moves the case that needs care to the front of the clinician's list while all other cases carry on. The check adds no device, no visit and no change to the model, and the decision stays with the clinician. The note explains the method in plain steps, shows how it speaks to the lighting and image-quality limitation named by the authors of the published model, and compares it with earlier work and patents. Keywords: survival prediction, face photograph, biological age, AI, uncertainty, robustness, early warning, shunting action, foundation model
