documents.abstract: In higher education, students’ needs are becoming increasingly diverse, making it insufficient to support them solely through general recommendations and traditional monitoring methods. Some students experience difficulties understanding course content, while others struggle with time management, organising independent learning, or adapting to the university environment. An important task of tutoring is to recognise these differences, maintain regular communication with students, and help them manage their own learning pathways consciously.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) has been rapidly developed and implemented in different sectors connected to computer vision and artificial intelligence due to the growth of the Internet and the prevalence of digital devices. An input picture can efficiently and effectively retrieve related images from a large-scale database. Over the last ten years, much work has been done to develop new CBIR theories and models, and numerous efficient CBIR algorithms have been developed. Finding identical pictures in an extensive collection that match the query picture is made more accessible through content-based image retrieval. Ranking the pictures for retrieval usually involves considering the representative feature similarities between the dataset and query pictures. This study introduces Deep Learning (DL)-based Opt-IncpResN-V2, a hyper-optimized framework designed to enhance image quality and enable feature-rich CBIR. With the proliferation of digital images and the expansion of image databases, efficient image retrieval methods are essential. Unlike traditional text-based image retrieval (TBIR), which relies on manual keyword annotation, CBIR retrieves images based on visual features such as colour, texture, and shape. Our framework incorporates an image quality improvement process during preprocessing, including noise reduction, edge detection, normalisation, and contrast enhancement. Features are extracted using the Inception-ResNet-V2 technique, and classification accuracy is improved using the Artificial Flora Optimisation Algorithm (AFOA). Images are then classified using DenseNet-264, and hyperparameters are optimised using the Improved Hippopotamus Optimisation Algorithm (IHOA). The proposed approach is evaluated on four benchmark datasets: Kvasir, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Corel-1k. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, achieving accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores exceeding 99% across all datasets.
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Mendalo Laut Village still face limitations in utilizing digital technology to support business identity development and promotion. This community service activity aimed to improve MSME actors’ understanding and provide practical experience in utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, as a tool for developing ideas and creating digital promotional materials. The activity was conducted on July 15, 2026, at the Mendalo Laut Village Office Hall and involved 16 MSME actors engaged in food and service businesses. The methods included material presentation, discussion, hands-on practice, and mentoring. Participants were introduced to the use of ChatGPT for developing prompts and creating concepts for business logos, posters, banners, and product flyers. The results showed that participants were enthusiastic about the training and gained initial experience in utilizing ChatGPT to support digital promotion. Some participants were able to follow the practical activities with guidance, while others required more intensive assistance due to differences in digital skills. This activity served as an initial step in encouraging the use of AI to support more independent and sustainable digital promotion among MSMEs.

Background Human oversight is widely treated as a safeguard for clinical artificial intelligence (AI), yet a reviewer may remain formally responsible without having the knowledge, time, or authority required to verify generated documentation. We develop “oversight asymmetry” as a prospective governance diagnosis and use neonatal discharge as a theoretical test context for responsible digital paediatrics, not as an observed setting of AI use. Methods We conducted a comparative-abductive, netnographically informed qualitative study of 64 public Reddit threads posted between 2021 and April 2026, with comment trees retrieved under pre-specified extraction parameters. The threads contained 2,848 comments and replies from 1,723 pseudonymised accounts in nursing, neonatal, paediatric, medicine, and health informatics communities, and 49 threads contributed to the final themes. A discharge and transition-home stream, drawn mainly from general nursing communities, and a smaller AI documentation and communication stream were analysed separately using reflexive thematic analysis before abductive comparison. Professional role was attributed only where contributors explicitly self-positioned. Results Discharge readiness was described as depending on knowledge distributed across records, professionals, bedside observation, and families, while responsibility for release could become concentrated. Frontline responsibility was separable from institutional authority, although several accounts described distributed oversight that worked because escalation was available. In four anchor threads from two communities, AI documentation discussions described faster drafting alongside residual source checking and correction, and a narrower set of accounts described reconstruction of missing clinical rationale. Workload accounts, together with AI-linked predictions in two threads, suggest that anticipated efficiency may be converted into higher workload before residual verification work is removed. We propose that oversight becomes vulnerable when verification responsibility and demand exceed epistemic access, protected time or consequential authority. Conclusion Oversight asymmetry identifies a prospective mechanism through which nominal human review may fail to constitute meaningful oversight. Responsible paediatric artificial intelligence governance should measure residual verification work, preserve provenance and access to family and bedside context, protect review time, and provide effective output-level and system-level escalation authority before automation is treated as additional capacity. The study generates propositions for prospective evaluation and does not claim that artificial intelligence-assisted neonatal discharge was directly observed.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Authorship can align three relations to a work: experiencing it as one’s own, feeling like the agent behind it, and standing answerable for it. Effortful engagement can support this alignment, an arrangement this article calls the labor nexus of authorship, but direction, selection, editing, and authority over release also matter. Generative artificial intelligence can separate initial-production effort from the resulting product without uniformly weakening ownership, agency, or responsibility. This conceptual analysis specifies an authorship legitimation deficit as a mismatch between a particular authorship designation and the experiential or contribution-based grounds expected to support it under prior domain criteria. Separate ownership, agency, and community-warrant profiles distinguish an unsupported sole-creator claim from a supported editorial role, even when the person’s contribution and experience are unchanged. Historical precedents locate the problem within delegated and distributed making. The main contribution is a role-relative conceptual classification. Conditional relational hypotheses concern refusal or qualification of authorship (P4) and later recognition of alternative contributions (P6); agency and observer credit-blame hypotheses (P5a/P5b) concern constituent concepts rather than effects of the deficit. Market dependence suppresses observable disavowal when qualification threatens income; perceived system agency conditions felt answerability while assigned release duties remain fixed. Contribution records may assist later recognition but do not guarantee it. The framework identifies when a role exceeds its grounds while preserving supported AI-assisted authorship and accountability for release.

Parental emotion regulation plays a critical role in shaping children's psychological adjustment, emotional resilience, and mental health outcomes. However, variations in cultural orientation, immigration experiences, family stress, and parenting practices complicate the identification of these relationships across immigrant and non-immigrant populations in the United States. This study proposes a novel Culturally Adaptive Parental Emotion Regulation and Mental Health Prediction Algorithm (CAPER-MH) to investigate the relationships between parental emotion regulation, cultural adaptation, family socioeconomic characteristics, and children's mental health. The proposed framework integrates multilevel statistical modelling, machine learning, and explainable artificial intelligence to estimate psychological risk while accounting for cultural heterogeneity and family-level dependencies. The study is designed to analyse parental emotion regulation difficulties, cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, acculturative stress, parent-child relationships, and children's internalizing and externalizing symptoms using validated psychometric instruments.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the travel industry has fundamentally redefined how organizations collaborate, compete, and deliver value. This chapter examines the various types of strategic alliances and partnerships that relate to AI-driven travel solutions, including the juristic relationships created when airlines and hotel chains, online travel agencies (OTAs), software providers, and startup companies, develop AI ecosystems together. Drawing on partnership theory, resource-based views, and platform economics, the research will explore how the motivations, structures, and governance models of these alliances. The research analyses the role of data sharing agreements, including partnership agreements, co-innovation labs, and intermediate integration of Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) as means of accelerating AI adoption and creating digital transformation. Last, the chapter will discuss such challenges as data privacy, competitive cannibalism, and trust asymmetries between competing legacy firms and technology operators.

Abstract Objective To compare patient trust in educational health contentand the physician providing it, when authorship is attributed to a physician or generative artificial intelligence (AI). Materials and Methods In a preregistered randomized, parallel survey study, participants read a health education article. Individuals were randomized to 1 of 4 conditions, attributing authorship of an identical article to (1) a physician author, (2) generative AI, (3) a physician assisted by AI (hybrid authorship), or (4) no author. Pregnant or postpartum English-speaking US adults (n = 400) were recruited in August-October 2025 via an online survey panel. Eighty percent passed timing and attention checks. Participants rated article engagement, content trust, and trust in the (hypothetical) recommending physician with Likert-scales. Bonferroni corrections were applied to post hoc pairwise comparisons (α = 0.05). Results Among participants who correctly recalled authorship (n = 195), AI-only authorship was associated with lower trust in content (mean, 9.43 vs 11.11; P = .001) and the recommending physician (mean, 8.93 vs 10.84; P = .03) compared with physician-only authorship, while hybrid authorship did not differ significantly from physician-only authorship for either outcome (content: P = .08; physician: P > .99). Sensitivity analyses including all participants (n = 321) were generally consistent with the primary findings. Engagement did not differ significantly across conditions in the primary analytic sample. Discussion As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into clinical care, how AI involvement and physician oversight are communicated to patients could have important implications for patient trust. Conclusion AI authorship was associated with reduced trust in patient-facing education despite identical, clinician-written content.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Akselerasi perkembangan teknologi Artificial Intelligence (AI) yang masif menuntut peningkatan kapasitas digital siswa kejuruan agar adaptif. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan literasi digital dan keterampilan praktis siswa SMK Semen Gresik dalam mengembangkan website menggunakan AI serta mengevaluasi luaran kodenya secara kritis. Metode pelaksanaan diorganisasikan melalui transfer pengetahuan dan demonstrasi perumusan instruksi (prompt engineering) berbasis kerangka CRAFT (Context, Role, Action, Format, Tone). Program ini diselenggarakan pada 24 April 2026 dengan melibatkan siswa konsentrasi keahlian Rekayasa Perangkat Lunak (RPL). Hasil kegiatan mengindikasikan bahwa pemanfaatan AI mampu mengakselerasi alur perancangan antarmuka dan arsitektur halaman web secara signifikan. Siswa terbukti mampu mentransformasikan kebutuhan spesifikasi pengguna menjadi prompt terstruktur serta melakukan refinasi dan modifikasi mandiri terhadap basis kode yang dihasilkan. Integrasi AI ini terbukti memperkokoh pemahaman logika automasi proses digital tanpa mengeliminasi kendali kognitif dan daya kritis siswa (human-in-the-loop) dalam siklus pengembangan perangkat lunak.

Blended learning supported by artificial intelligence offers an alternative approach to improving students’ learning outcomes in Information and Communication Technology (ICT). However, the combined use of blended learning and MagicSchool AI for digital literacy instruction at the junior high school level requires further empirical investigation. This study aimed to analyze the effect of a blended learning model supported by MagicSchool AI on seventh-grade students’ ICT learning outcomes at SMPI Al Ishlah Bukittinggi. The study employed a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design. The participants comprised 56 students divided into experimental and control groups, with 28 students in each group. Data were collected through achievement tests administered before and after the intervention and analyzed using an independent-samples t test. The results showed that the experimental group’s mean score increased from 51.07 on the pretest to 81.96 on the posttest, while the control group’s mean score increased from 53.39 to 67.50. Hypothesis testing revealed a significant difference in learning outcomes between the two groups (p < .001). These findings provide empirical support for the potential of blended learning supported by MagicSchool AI to improve students’ learning outcomes in digital literacy. In practical terms, the findings may inform teachers’ design of ICT instruction that integrates face-to-face activities and the use of artificial intelligence. Future research should involve more schools and compare the contributions of individual instructional components to clarify their roles in students’ attainment of learning outcomes.

Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work. Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly. When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others. Four studies provide evidence for “empathy offloading”: when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it. When AI seems more capable of empathy, people—both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)—report more empathy offloading. When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others’ mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses and more social judgment (Study 4). Empathic AI might provide emotional support at any time, but it may weaken our ethical and emotional commitments to fellow human beings. The implications of offloading emotional support may include empathic devaluing and atrophy, moral deskilling, and societal fraying.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: Purpose Drawing on job demands–resources theory, this study examines how perceived algorithmic operations control (PAC) relates to couriers' safety-compliance risk. PAC denotes algorithmic oversight: feeling monitored, directed and constrained by platform algorithms. The risk is physical: unsafe riding that can cause crashes. Two mechanisms are tested: system-triggered interruptions that fragment attention (a job demand) and reduced autonomy to adapt safely (a lost resource). Boundary conditions are dependence on platform income and visibility-based transparency, a widely advocated remedy. Design/methodology/approach In an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, interviews and field observations informed the measures. A cross-sectional questionnaire survey of 344 food-delivery couriers in China was analysed using regression-based moderated-mediation tests. Riders' forum posts, produced independently of the survey, served to triangulate (cross-check) the survey constructs. Findings Stronger PAC is associated with more self-reported risky riding (incidents were not measured), partly through more interruptions and lower autonomy. Economic dependence weakens the interruption pathway but strengthens autonomy loss. Transparency strengthens both pathways, linking PAC to more interruptions and greater autonomy loss. This is the transparency paradox: a presumed remedy unintentionally amplifies risk. Originality/value Algorithmic management operates through adjustable system parameters: how often platform data interrupt couriers and how much discretion they retain. To cut risk without losing efficiency, platforms can pace notifications, freeze mid-route reassignments, restore discretion through exception handling and pair transparency with actionable options. For regulators, disclosure mandates alone may not make delivery safer.

University faculty members’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is important to the digital transformation of higher education, yet the motivational mechanisms associated with such behavior remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), and the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study used a sample of 374 university faculty members to examine, through a moderated mediation model, the mechanism underlying the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and AI technology adoption behavior. The results showed that perceived craftsmanship spirit significantly and positively predicted AI technology adoption behavior and that work engagement mediated this relationship. Challenge stressors negatively moderated the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and work engagement and weakened the mediating effect of work engagement. These findings reveal the underlying pathway through which perceived craftsmanship spirit promotes AI technology adoption behavior and provide theoretical and practical implications for advancing the digital development and transformation of higher education.

BACKGROUND Virtual patients (VPs) are widely used in medical education, but creating high-quality cases requires clinical expertise, iterative revision, and alignment with educational objectives. Generative AI may support VP authoring, but direct comparisons between AI-generated and clinician-developed cases delivered within the same educational setting remain limited. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to compare medical students’ learner-perceived ratings of 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed virtual cardiology patient scenario with those of 1 clinician-developed virtual cardiology patient scenario delivered through the same mobile platform. METHODS A randomized, participant-blinded 2-arm controlled study was conducted in October 2025 during scheduled fifth-year emergency medicine course sessions. Eligible participants were fifth-year medical students who had completed the cardiology course. Students were assigned 1:1 to complete either a clinician-developed VP (CD-VP; n=64) or a ChatGPT-generated VP (GPT-VP; n=67). Both scenarios followed a shared acute coronary syndrome blueprint and were delivered through the same mobile-optimized app (mobile VPs app [MobiViP]) with identical interface structure and branching logic. The GPT-VP was generated using GPT-5 and refined through iterative follow-up prompting under expert review; direct manual rewriting was prohibited. After completion, students completed a mandatory 19-item questionnaire covering realism and validity, cognitive load, self-reported learning and reflection, and engagement and satisfaction. Analyses included reliability testing, 1-sample tests against a neutral midpoint, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Spearman correlations. Full scenario content and development details are provided as multimedia appendices. RESULTS A total of 131 complete questionnaires were analyzed, with no item-level missing data. Mean subscale scores in the CD-VP group were 3.81 (SD 0.64) for realism and validity, 3.67 (SD 0.74) for cognitive load, 3.64 (SD 0.73) for self-reported learning and reflection, and 4.16 (SD 0.64) for engagement and satisfaction; corresponding GPT-VP scores were 4.11 (SD 0.56), 3.03 (SD 0.76), 3.86 (SD 0.77), and 4.28 (SD 0.58), respectively. Compared with the CD-VP, the GPT-VP received higher ratings for realism and validity (Mann-Whitney U=1503.0; P=.003) and lower cognitive load ratings, indicating a lower perceived burden (Mann-Whitney U=1070.5; P<.001). Self-reported learning and reflection showed a marginal difference between groups, with a higher rating for the GPT-VP (Mann-Whitney U=1719.0; P=.05), whereas engagement and satisfaction did not differ significantly (Mann-Whitney U=1922.5; P=.31). Internal consistency was acceptable to good for most subscales, although internal consistency for the realism and validity subscale in the GPT-VP group was moderate (Cronbach α=0.67). CONCLUSIONS In this single-center randomized study, 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed cardiology VP scenario was rated similarly to or more favorably than 1 clinician-developed scenario in selected learner-perceived domains. Future research should expand to objective learning, retention, development workload, and scalability outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The fast adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism management has fundamentally changed the way organizations handle human resources, performance, and utilize workforce data. This chapter explains how AI-based performance management systems and workforce analytics can be used in a versatile way in the tourism and hospitality industries. It relies on current empirical data and theoretical ideas to explore how machine learning algorithms, predictive analytics, and real-time data platforms are changing talent acquisition, employee performance appraisal, demand-based scheduling, and strategic workforce planning. The chapter also discusses the ethical issues of algorithmic bias, privacy, and employee autonomy, and the need to adopt hybrid human-AI governance frameworks. The practical implementation results are reflected in the case studies of large global tourism enterprises. The chapter ends with a discussion of future research directions and policy implications of sustainable, technology-enhanced people management in tourism.

Severe bleeding remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in cardiac surgery, and hemostatic blood components, mainly platelet concentrates and fresh frozen plasma, are essential to perioperative hemostatic management. While restrictive strategies for packed red blood cell transfusions are now well established within Patient Blood Management, inappropriate prophylactic transfusions of these hemostatic therapies continue to receive less attention. This narrative review investigates variations in hemostatic therapy among centres for adult cardiac surgery, and examines the factors that might explain these differences. A review of fourteen original studies involving nearly 220,000 patients from over 1,000 centres worldwide revealed significant variations in platelet and fresh-frozen plasma transfusion rates across centres. Differences in patient and procedural characteristics cannot entirely explain these variations. Although viscoelastic hemostatic tests have improved bedside assessment and lowered exposure in some settings, they have not eradicated significant variations in practice. The available evidence indicates that hospital culture, local organization, transfusion thresholds, and human factors all have an impact on transfusion behaviour. Optimizing the use of hemostatic therapies in adult cardiac surgery will therefore not only require better tools and protocols, but also increased focus on the organizational and non-technical factors that influence decision-making.

Autopsy, as a cornerstone of post-mortem investigation, has undergone significant evolution over the years. Traditional autopsy, characterised by manual examination and tissue sampling, has long been the gold standard for determining the cause of death and uncovering underlying pathologies. However, the emergence of digital autopsy, leveraging advanced imaging techniques and computational analysis, presents a promising alternative. This chapter provides a comprehensive comparison between traditional and digital autopsy, encompassing their methodologies, diagnostic accuracy, practicality, limitations, and ethical considerations. It focuses on how digital tools such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and digital imaging and communications in medicine (DICOM)-based visualisation reconstruct the human body’s structure into detailed, colour-coded three-dimensional models of the internal organs. The chapter further examines the impact of technological advancement on forensic pathology and explores the integration of digitalisation, artificial intelligence, and minimally invasive techniques into routine post-mortem practice. Its novelty lies in bringing conventional dissection-based autopsy and digital/virtual autopsy together within a single comparative framework, and in extending that framework to artificial intelligence and minimally invasive sampling. By elucidating the strengths and limitations of both approaches, it aims to guide forensic practitioners, pathologists, radiologists, policymakers, and researchers in making informed decisions regarding post-mortem examination methodologies. The chapter moves from foundational definitions through a technique-by-technique comparison to ethical and future considerations, and is intended primarily for forensic medicine trainees, pathologists, and medico-legal professionals.

Modern teams depend on PostgreSQL for mission-critical workloads, yet administration is still done by hand-writing SQL in disconnected tools such as psql, pgAdmin and DBeaver, while AI assistants such as GitHub Copilot have no live connection to the database and cannot read its schema, execution plans or error output. LLM-generated SQL also introduces new injection-style security risks. This paper presents PGNexus-AI, a PostgreSQL-only desktop IDE that combines Google Gemini, Gemma 4 and GitHub Copilot behind a schema-grounded orchestration layer. It provides natural-language-to-SQL generation, execution-plan-driven query optimization, automatic error diagnosis and correction, and AI-generated schema documentation with column-relationship mapping. A defense-in-depth safety layer (parameterization, query preview and confirmation, read-only and sandbox execution, role-based scoping and injection screening) protects production databases, and GitHub integration version-controls SQL and migrations. We describe the architecture, methodology and an evaluation plan covering efficiency, reliability, optimization and security.

Pharmaceutical quality assurance (QA) is a comprehensive and systematic approach designed to ensure that medicinal products consistently meet predetermined standards of quality, safety, identity, strength, purity and efficacy throughout their intended lifecycle. The contemporary pharmaceutical industry has moved beyond a predominantly end-product testing model toward integrated, science-based and risk-based quality management. Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), Pharmaceutical Quality Systems (PQS), Quality Risk Management (QRM), Quality by Design (QbD), validation, qualification, change control, deviation management, corrective and preventive action (CAPA), supplier qualification, documentation and data integrity constitute major components of modern pharmaceutical QA. International regulatory frameworks developed by the World Health Organization (WHO), International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and other regulatory bodies increasingly emphasize lifecycle management, continual improvement and reliable data. The 2024 tenth edition of the WHO pharmaceutical quality assurance compendium provides an updated global framework extending from pharmaceutical development and manufacturing to quality control and post-marketing surveillance. Recent advances in digitalization, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), Process Analytical Technology (PAT), continuous manufacturing and advanced data analytics are further transforming pharmaceutical quality management. However, these technologies also introduce challenges related to validation, data integrity, cyber security, model governance and regulatory acceptance. This review discusses the fundamental concepts, major components, regulatory framework, implementation strategies, current challenges and emerging trends in pharmaceutical quality assurance. An integrated lifecycle-based QA system supported by scientific understanding, risk management, robust documentation, quality culture and appropriate technology is essential for ensuring consistent product quality and protecting patient safety.

Interindividual variability in drug response represents a persistent challenge in clinical pharmacology, contributing to therapeutic failure and adverse drug reactions (ADRs) in a substantial proportion of patients. Pharmacogenomics, the study of how genomic variation influences drug disposition and effects, has emerged as a transformative discipline bridging pharmacology and genomics.This review synthesizes contemporary evidence regarding the principles, clinical applications, technologies, and implementation frameworks of pharmacogenomics within the broader context of personalized medicine. Genetic polymorphisms affecting pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic pathways—particularly within cytochrome P450 enzymes, thiopurine methyltransferase, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, and human leukocyte antigen loci—demonstrate robust associations with drug efficacy and toxicity. Regulatory agencies including the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) have incorporated pharmacogenomic biomarkers into drug labeling, while the Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) and the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group (DPWG) have issued actionable dosing guidelines for numerous gene-drug pairs. Despite compelling evidence, the transition from research to routine clinical practice remains heterogeneous globally, impeded by economic barriers, educational gaps, and ethical complexities surrounding genetic data.The integration of artificial intelligence, multi-omics platforms, and digital health infrastructure promises to accelerate pharmacogenomic adoption, yet successful implementation requires harmonized regulatory standards, equitable access across diverse populations, and systematic healthcare professional education. Pharmacogenomics stands poised to fundamentally redefine therapeutic paradigms, shifting from empirical prescribing to genotype-directed precision medicine.

Nature-based solutions (NBS) are a promising strategy for building climate resilience, but their implementation requires land. Realising NBS on private land, which holds great potential, remains a challenge. Aligning landowner interests with climate adaptation goals lies within the realm of land policy. However, studies show that traditional land policy instruments are often ineffective when applied to NBS and private land. Cooperative approaches that engage landowners directly are needed – but they raise new questions: How do we find landowners willing to implement NBS and engage them effectively? This research focuses on landowners who are primarily motivated by non-financial interests to implement NBS. These dynamics are explored through a qualitative case-study-based research design, focused on NBS implementers across Austria, Czechia, Germany, Italy, Romania, and Slovakia. Initial results indicate different types of landowners (homeowners, farmers, company owners) have distinct interests in implementing NBS. While economic incentives play a role, intrinsic motivations mainly shape landowners’ decisions. This underscores the need for tailored solutions considering diverse intrinsic motivations. Effective NBS implementation strategies must strengthen intrinsic motivations, build trust, and respect landowner autonomy.

This study examined the effects of physical activity (PA) guideline adherence on physical fitness, hypoglycemia awareness, and glycemic control in young adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), framing PA adherence as a behavioral nudge toward selfmanagement. METHODS:This cross-sectional study analyzed 108 young adults with T2DM (aged 20-44 years), categorized into two groups based on PA guideline adherence: those meeting guidelines (G-Met; ≥150 min/week of moderate-to-vigorous PA, n=52) and those not meeting guidelines (G-Unmet; <150 min/week, n=56).Lower-body muscle strength, flexibility, hypoglycemia awareness, and HbA1c levels were assessed.Between-group differences were examined using independent t-tests, and independent predictors of HbA1c and hypoglycemia awareness were identified via multiple linear regression. RESULTS:The G-Met group demonstrated significantly greater lower-body muscle strength (p=.003) and flexibility (p=.018) compared with the G-Unmet group.Additionally, the G-Met group reported significantly higher awareness of hypoglycemia causes, including excessive PA (p=.037) and insufficient food intake (p=.014).Multiple linear regression confirmed that PA guideline adherence was independently associated with higher hypoglycemia awareness (p=.021).Although HbA1c levels did not differ significantly between groups, multiple regression analysis identified lower-body muscle strength as a factor independently associated with lower HbA1c (β=-0.343,p=.043).CONCLUSIONS: Adherence to PA guidelines was associated with improved physical fitness and greater hypoglycemia awareness in young adults with T2DM.Importantly, higher levels of lower-body muscle strength, associated with PA guideline adherence, were independently associated with better glycemic control, suggesting that regular PA functions as a behavioral nudge that simultaneously builds physiological capacity and promotes cognitive engagement in diabetes self-management.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly recommend cultural venues and tell visitors why, but such explanations can be plausible without being faithful. We report a preregistered counterfactual audit of four commercial LLMs recommending venues in three Greek destinations. Each model received structured visitor profiles based on the ACUX typology and a fixed, fact-checked catalogue of 20 venues, and returned three ranked recommendations with explanations. One profile attribute was changed at a time, and every change was measured against the variation between identical requests (4,032 calls). For every model, attributes cited in explanations were associated with larger changes in recommendations, but only moderately (counterfactual faithfulness score 0.26–0.42). Age, gender and nationality were almost never cited and had small effects that did not survive correction for multiple tests. Explanations often described venue properties absent from the catalogue (29–83%), whereas fabricated visitor preferences were rare (4–14%). When a poorly matching venue was imposed, two models seldom disclosed the mismatch (3% and 13%) and the other two did so in 53% and 79% of cases. Judge-rated plausibility declined only modestly, although agreement with human ratings was low. LLM explanations of cultural recommendations should be treated as persuasive text and checked against the information the system holds.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

BackgroundErgonomic problems are common in the field of dentistry due to musculoskeletal and neurological conditions that occur in various parts of the body as a result of poor posture and repetitive movements.ObjectivesTo analyze ergonomic errors by clinical area among dental students at a private university in Cusco.MethodsA cross-sectional observational study using secondary data was conducted, involving a population of 182 students selected according to specific criteria. A sample of 150 students from different areas of the dental clinic at a private university in Cusco, corresponding to the seventh, eighth, and ninth semesters, was analyzed. The RULA and REBA ergonomic scales were applied as assessment tools.ResultsThe study revealed that poor postures predominated in the pediatric dentistry clinical area across the five dimensions analyzed, followed by endodontics, restorative dentistry, periodontics, and oral rehabilitation.ConclusionsThere is a high prevalence of poor posture among dental students, highlighting the need for ergonomic education and preventive measures to reduce musculoskeletal injuries and improve the well-being of future dentists, regardless of their specialty.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.

Abstract Background With the development of artificial intelligence technique, machine learning (ML) algorithms have been widely applied to forecast outcomes of various diseases. Current study aimed to investigate the potential utility of machine learning algorithms for predicting postoperative persistent shoulder pain (PSP) and to investigate the related risk factors following rotator cuff repair surgery. Materials and methods A cohort of 491 patients with rotator cuff tears who had undergone surgical intervention was enrolled and analyzed. Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score of ≥4 at one year follow-up was defined as indicative of ongoing shoulder pain. Consequently, patients were classified into a residual pain group and a pain-free group. Nine commonly used machine learning models were trained to distinguish between patients with residual pain and those without. Furthermore, the three models that exhibited the highest predictive performance were combined into a single ensemble of the nine models to improve the classification of patients with residual pain versus those without. The area under the curve (AUC), specificity, sensitivity and accuracy were calculated for each model to evaluate their predictive capabilities. A prespecified LASSO-based feature-selection strategy was used to identify candidate clinical variables, with additional stability analyses (forward selection, exhaustive search) reported in the Supplementary Materials. Variables consistently selected were considered candidate risk factors for PSP in patients. Results (1) Machine learning models demonstrated their effectiveness in classifying patients with postoperative pain. The predictive performance was notably enhanced using an ensemble learning technique. Among the models, the Support Vector Machine (SVM) exhibited the highest accuracy when serving as the aggregator. (2) The ensemble learning models identified several critical predictive factors, including the Fear of Pain Questionnaire, the Pain Catastrophizing Scale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)-Perceived Sleep Quality, the Central Sensitization Inventory, and the Pain Surface Body Chart score. Conclusion Our findings suggest that a stacking ensemble of preoperative psychosocial variables, developed and internally validated in this single-center retrospective cohort, shows promise for preliminary risk stratification of clinically significant shoulder pain at one year after rotator cuff repair. These hypothesis-generating results require multicenter external validation before clinical use. Level of evidence Level 4, Diagnosis. Clinical trial number Not applicable. This was a retrospective observational study and was not registered as a clinical trial.

This Perspective article examines the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) initiatives to strengthen artificial intelligence (AI) and cyber security governance and explores their potential to reinforce nuclear security in Southeast Asia. It argues that as digital technologies become increasingly embedded in nuclear facilities and supply chains, integrating cyber security into nuclear security frameworks is imperative. The study recommends the development of a regional action plan or roadmap to (i) embed cyber security more systematically into nuclear security policies, (ii) deepen cooperation among ASEAN member states, and (iii) raise awareness of the AI–cyber–nuclear security nexus among industry, civil society, and academia. The paper also highlights the roles of key regional and international actors, including the ASEAN Network of Regulatory Bodies on Atomic Energy (ASEANTOM), ASEAN cyber security institutions, AI safety think tanks, and Track II expert networks, in advancing cooperation and knowledge-sharing in this emerging domain. Drawing on the author’s experience with the Nuclear Energy Experts Group of the Council for Security Cooperation in the Asia-Pacific (CSCAP), the paper illustrates how Track II dialogues have facilitated the identification of AI–cyber–nuclear security risks, raised awareness among policymakers, scientists, and academics, and informed ongoing discussions on enhancing nuclear security governance in Southeast Asia.

Conditions, optimizer protocol, hypotheses and analysis plan for the annotation-harness arm (Claude Sonnet 5.5 as coder, Claude Opus 5.5 as optimizer) of a study on reaching human-level agreement (Cohen's kappa) with LLM coding of teacher talk moves. Registered before any condition of this arm was evaluated on the validation or test part. Part 1 (sampling rule and data split): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23727437.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Automated assessment of second-language (L2) writing supports language teaching and testing by providing rapid, consistent scores across multiple rubric dimensions. We study whether small, openly available language models can be turned into reliable analytic raters, and we introduce PROSE, a rubric-aware, multi-objective fine-tuning method built on a compact DeBERTa-v3 encoder with low-rank adaptation. PROSE trains a regression read-out together with a soft-ordinal auxiliary head, and combines a squared-error term for calibration, a distance-aware soft-ordinal term that respects the ordered rubric bands, a concordance term that restores the spread of human ratings and improves agreement with human ratings, and a trait-relational coherence term. On the ELLIPSE corpus of L2 English essays, PROSE raises the quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.646 for a strong regression baseline to 0.661—a small but statistically reliable gain under a paired test across folds (mean difference +0.015—95% CI [0.007,0.023], and paired t-test p=0.007; p=0.030 after correcting for the overlap between cross-validation training sets), with comparable error and improvements on all seven scoring dimensions, four of which remain significant after Holm correction, and on the Write & Improve (BEA-2019) proficiency data, it matches the strongest baseline on agreement and accuracy and clearly outperforms classification and pure ordinal training. Zero-shot prompting of three strong large language models (GPT-5.4, Claude-Sonnet-4-6, DeepSeek-Chat) reaches a kappa of only 0.13 to 0.21 on the same essays, and a distributional analysis shows that the tested large models produce compressed score distributions with means below the human mean, while the compact fine-tuned model reproduces the human score distribution. Further analyses show that the gain is stable under reasonable changes of the loss weights and holds for truncated and non-truncated essays and across gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic, and grade groups, although these analyses also reveal a shared grade-related bias and a reliance on length and lexical-diversity cues that call for caution in deployment. The results indicate that, for this task, a task-specific objective applied to a small supervised model is far more effective than general-purpose models used zero-shot; we are careful to attribute the gap to task-specific supervision and objective design rather than to model scale alone.

Background India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is building a national digital health ecosystem. Uptake by health care providers remains uneven. Paper records often persist alongside digital tools, suggesting a gap between tool design and frontline care. Objectives To explore how health care providers and other stakeholders in two Indian states experience the usability of digital health tools under ABDM, how far they trust these tools, and what shapes their adoption in routine practice. Methods We analysed 42 in-depth interviews with state and district officials, frontline health workers, clinicians and implementation partners in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Interviews were collected under the provider adoption objective of the parent Digital Health Exemplars: India study. We used template analysis, with Cognitive Load Theory and Human Factors Engineering as a priori lenses. The themes were then mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Results We identified six mismatches between tool design and clinical reality. These were (1) rigid interfaces that clash with nonlinear clinical reasoning, (2) separate portals that force repeated data entry, (3) fears of surveillance and unclear data use by AI tools, (4) reliance on paper and WhatsApp as practical workarounds, (5) unreliable networks, devices and power, and (6) one-time, generic training. In some settings, use appeared to depend on incentives and partner support. Conclusion Providers in this study did not avoid digital tools because of low digital literacy alone. They avoided tools that added work without clinical value. Sustained adoption under ABDM is likely to need interoperable, offline-capable tools, clear data-use safeguards and cadre-specific training, addressed in national implementation guidance alongside enrolment targets.

Anxiety and depression are major contributors to the global disease burden; however, fewer than half of patients treated with standard pharmacotherapy achieve sustained remission. This gap underscores the need to identify effective adjunctive treatments. The bidirectional gut-brain axis offers a valuable perspective by linking diet to neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis reactivity. This framework positions nutritional psychiatry as a complement, rather than a substitute, for established care. This narrative review examines three converging intervention classes: psychobiotics, dietary polyphenols, and precision nutraceuticals. Randomized trials of Lactobacillus helveticus R0052, Bifidobacterium longum R0175, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 demonstrate modest but reproducible reductions in depressive and anxiety symptoms, although effect sizes vary. Plausible mechanisms include reduced low-grade neuroinflammation, partial normalization of HPA axis reactivity, and a shift in tryptophan metabolism from the kynurenine pathway toward serotonin synthesis—although human evidence supporting these pathways remains limited. Polyphenol biology introduces an additional dimension. Microbial conversion of ellagitannins, isoflavones, and lignans into urolithin A, equol, and enterolactone can alter the bioavailability of neuroactive metabolites. Consequently, an individual’s metabotype likely accounts for some of the variability in clinical response. We propose that microbiota-guided strategies—stratified by enterotype, metabotype, tryptophan–kynurenine flux, and short-chain fatty acid output—could significantly enhance psychiatric care. Multi-omic profiling and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven digital phenotyping can operationalize this precision approach. However, methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, inconsistent strain and dose reporting, and regulatory ambiguity continue to hinder translation, as recent meta-analyses highlight.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist teachers with organizing information, generating alternatives, and drafting feedback. Its use in consequential judgments requires verifiable evidence and professional oversight. This study examines how teachers regulate optional GenAI assistance while preserving professional judgment. Methods Research on felt accountability, metacognitive monitoring, and AI literacy is conceptually integrated to develop a psychological process model of teacher decision episodes. Governance clarity is specified through rule clarity and role clarity, with responsible GenAI decision-making defined as regulated decision conduct. Results The conceptual analysis produces five testable propositions and one configurational expectation. Governance clarity is proposed to support responsible conduct through perceived accountability. Decision uncertainty is modeled as a metacognitive signal whose behavioral value depends on calibration and regulation; AI literacy is specified as a resource for verification, calibrated reliance, and appropriate escalation. Responsible conduct encompasses appropriate delegation, verification, calibrated reliance and accountable human authority, traceability, and escalation or override. These model outputs are theoretical propositions, not empirically established effects. Discussion The framework distinguishes generative assistance from conventional algorithmic advice and identifies task-dependent applications in assessment, feedback, referral, and student support. Future tests should compare unaided and assisted judgment, distinguish process quality from decision accuracy, and examine stakes, reversibility, and contextual dependence. Teachers retain authority to accept, modify, or reject GenAI output, or proceed without GenAI assistance.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) into Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) has raised pivotal questions regarding their psychometric validity, construct representation, and rater consistency in second language (L2) writing assessment. While LLMs offer scalable scoring and feedback capabilities, empirical evidence regarding their susceptibility to systematic scoring drifts across nuanced analytical criteria remains scarce. This calibration study benchmarks three frontier LLMs—GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro—against an expert human gold standard using the multidimensional LICA framework (Language, Ideas, Cohesion, and Academic Appropriateness). Utilizing a rigorous psychometric pipeline spanning ordinal alignment (Quadratic Weighted Kappa [QWK] and Mean Absolute Error [MAE]), inter-rater reliability (two-way random-effects "ICC" [2,1]), systematic scoring bias (Bland–Altman agreement limits), and multi-rater consensus (Fleiss’ κ), we evaluated model behaviors across a calibrated corpus of L2 academic essays (N total =20 rating instances per model). Empirical findings demonstrate marked dimension-dependent divergence in automated assessment: GPT-4o achieved deterministic concordance with expert ratings ("QWK"=1.000, "MAE"=0.000, "ICC"=1.000, and zero directional bias: d ̅=0.000), faithfully replicating human evaluative criteria. Claude 3.5 Sonnet displayed robust ordinal reliability ("QWK"=0.949, "ICC"=0.966), yet exhibited a systematic leniency drift localized to Cohesion and Academic Appropriateness (d ̅=+0.100, "MAE"=0.100). Gemini 1.5 Pro manifested a pronounced severity drift across Language, Ideas, and Appropriateness (d ̅=-0.250, "MAE"=0.250, "QWK"=0.925, "ICC"=0.947). Crucially, autonomous multi-model consensus reached substantial agreement on overt structural and conceptual dimensions (Ideas: κ=0.643; Cohesion: κ=0.643; Language: κ=0.545), but degraded considerably on Academic Appropriateness (κ=0.286, fair agreement). These results reveal a fundamental construct dissociation: while current generative LLMs reliably evaluate codified linguistic and rhetorical patterns, they struggle to consistently appraise sociopragmatic nuance, epistemic stance, and contextual register conventions. The study cautions TESOL practitioners and assessment developers against treating LLM ratings as monolithic constructs, highlighting the critical imperative of dimension-specific rater calibration and human-in-the-loop oversight in high-stakes L2 writing evaluation and formative automated feedback systems.

People learn to play musical instruments in various ways – from being totally self-taught through acquiring skills within the social architecture of friendship groups all the way to training in formal conservatoires. My own journey began with naïve attempts to copy my favourite bands and replicate their music through imitation. Lucy Green’s seminal work How Popular Musicians Learn: A Way Ahead for Music Education (2017) highlights the stark differences between popular and classical musicians in terms of pedagogical approaches, learning environments and music-making processes. Green argues that popular musicians primarily learn through informal, self-directed processes, which contrast starkly with the formalised, structured education which is typical of classical musicians. She notes that popular musicians often start out by playing along with recordings and figuring out songs by ear rather than relying on written notation. This aural tradition emphasises imitation, experimentation and personal discovery, allowing musicians to develop their musicality in a highly personal and intuitive manner. Claire described this organic evolution when recalling the start of her own musical journey: My dad had really good taste in music… . It was through him. I had a record player in my room and I sang. I loved the singing – I sang at school and assemblies. I just remember that from a really young age. I didn’t come from a musical family – none of my family could play instruments – but it was always there. I just knew that I enjoyed it. It was just something that I kept wanting to do. Gloria similarly experienced an irresistible urge to music for its own sake in her youth: I just go back to when I was sitting on my bed when I should have been writing an English essay, noodling on my guitar, writing a song – and it wasn’t to get famous. And it wasn’t for the internet – that wasn’t even a thing. Popular musicians typically engage in what Green describes as ‘enculturation’: a process by which we absorb the music around us, often from a very young age, by listening to and imitating our favourite artists. This process is mostly informal, driven by intrinsic motivation, meaning that we choose what we want to learn and play, rather than anyone else imposing their choices upon us. In other words, we are guided by our own musical tastes and aspirations.

Ranking aggregation from multiple retrievers is a powerful yet under-explored technique in modern retrieval and RAG systems. We introduce LLM-IRA, the first extension of the quantum-inspired interactive ranking aggregation framework to document reranking. By leveraging large language models (LLMs) solely for pairwise judgments on high-disagreement document pairs, our method learns fusion weights in a principled, interactive way. The final ranking is a simple, ultra-fast pointwise linear fusion of scores, no full pairwise matrix or expensive listwise prompting is required. Experiments on the BEIR benchmark and TREC Deep Learning tracks with an open-weight instruction-tuned judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) show that LLM-IRA matches or numerically exceeds strong static fusion baselines on 5 of 6 evaluated benchmarks. We report two weight-update variants: momentum blending and a full accumulated-history refit, which together reach statistical significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05) over the best unsupervised aggregator on 4 of 6 benchmarks (DL19 under momentum; DL20, DBpedia, and NFCorpus under accumulated refit, which is the stronger of the two configurations overall). On the benchmarks we profiled (DL19, DL20), it already clears the best unsupervised baseline within as few as 5 LLM calls per query, well before exhausting its typical ~25--30 call budget. LLM-IRA also achieves cost-effectiveness comparable to state-of-the-art zero-shot LLM rerankers at an order of magnitude fewer LLM calls, and requires no training data or model fine-tuning.

BACKGROUND: Adult intensive care units (ICUs) generate a persistent acoustic burden from alarms, care activity, equipment and communication. This burden can undermine patient rest and contribute to alarm fatigue, cognitive workload and distress among nurses. AIM: To present a nursing-led conceptual framework for addressing alarm-related acoustic burden in adult critical care. STUDY DESIGN: Literature-informed conceptual analysis. A structured purposive evidence map was audited using two PubMed searches run on 9 September 2026 (3377 unique records after PMID deduplication) and citation checking. Twenty-nine selected sources were charted against the five domains. This was not a systematic review; no original data, formal consensus or framework validation was undertaken. RESULTS: QUIET Care proposes five connected practice domains: quantify and qualify the sound environment; use patient-specific monitoring and alarms; integrate quiet into workflow; engage people and culture; and track, test and learn. It treats the domains as locally adaptable hypotheses and requires explicit safety balancing measures. CONCLUSIONS: QUIET Care is a pragmatic proposal for local co-design and evaluation, not a validated intervention or universal sound target. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: The framework may help critical care nurses and leaders organise source mapping, alarm customisation, workflow redesign, team ownership and small safety-monitored tests of change while preserving the audibility of urgent alerts.

By combining the artificial intelligence (AI) and human experts knowledge is changing the way of how work isdesigned and executed. This is different from traditional automation techniques that only handle routine , regular tasks asHuman-AI Collaboration integrates the speed and analysis capability of machines with human decision-making, empathy, andethical oversight. This paper looks at recent studies on HAIC. It finds three major problems: Future-oriented thinking ,differences between sectors and how to manage things together. It also propose a five-level system for arranging tasks, calculatingtrust, keeping human control, and checking ethics. The framework is studied using three case studies about customer support,management consulting, software development. It looks at tradeoffs, effects on workers, and rules. The evidence shows that whentasks are easy for AI, can be changed beyond what AI can do, and always need human checks, there are big benefits. The papersays that the future of work will involve teamwork between humans and AI, working together in a cycle with feedback. Thisframework is just an idea and has not been tried in a real company.

The advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) technology has revolutionized the digital marketing sector, yet its impact on consumer psychology requires deeper understanding. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach based on the Scopus database, this study analyzes the relationships among GenAI usage, customer engagement, and customer trust. Literature mapping reveals that current research focuses on four primary clusters: consumer behavioral dynamics and purchase intentions, visual quality (hyperrealism), transparency and ethical issues, and collaborative creativity efficiency. Based on an analysis of these findings, the study identifies an "Authenticity Paradox," wherein AI-generated hyperrealistic visuals effectively boost purchase intentions but risk triggering the "uncanny valley" effect thereby undermining consumer trust if transparency is lacking. Trust is significantly shaped by the interplay between drivers, such as transparent labeling (watermarking), and inhibitors, such as visual artifacts and privacy concerns. Regarding engagement effectiveness, AI proves superior in stimulating interaction among existing followers, whereas human-generated content remains essential for reaching new audiences due to its empathy and emotional resonance. The study concludes that adopting a hybrid marketing strategy specifically Human-AI Co-Creation represents the optimal approach for synergizing GenAI's technological efficiency with the authenticity of the human touch in the long term.

documents.abstract: The education of university students requires strategies that link literary reading with personality development. Objective: To present reflections on the management of literary works with educational content for the personality development of university students, based on articles from partner journals—the Cuban Journal of Information Sciences in Health and Islands—located with the support of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and compared with academic literature. Methodology: A qualitative, descriptive-propositive approach was adopted. The proposal was evaluated through consultation with eight professionals in the educational field, including teachers and administrators, intentionally selected for their experience in higher education, reading promotion, and academic management. Results: The reflections were organized into four dimensions: reading and educational diagnosis, selection of works with educational content, planning and allocation of resources, and evaluation of educational outcomes. The proposal highlights the need to coordinate libraries, faculty, and administrative teams to promote reading practices linked to values, empathy, self-esteem, and critical thinking. Conclusion/Contributions: The educational management of literary works can contribute to the development of university students' personalities when accompanied by clear objectives, teacher guidance, administrator participation, and periodic evaluation.
